strengths: Addresses a relevant NLP problem: forecasting pretraining loss and understanding its dependence on token position. The proposed equations provide an interpretable empirical model.
The positional reciprocal relationship has substantial descriptive support: reported R² exceeds 0.95 for over 99% of checkpoints, with observations across two model sizes and two evaluation datasets.

The experiments include 400B-token training runs, frequent checkpoints, forecasts from multiple training prefixes, and weighting comparisons across eight downstream benchmarks. Figure 1 shows promising improvements over the tested forecasting baselines.
weaknesses: The central forecasting claim needs more independent validation. Section 3.3 selects the functional forms and transition point using complete training trajectories, while Figure 1 does not clearly identify runs held out from these design choices. Fitting coefficients only on early checkpoints does not remove future-informed model selection. Fixing the method on development runs and evaluating unseen runs would strengthen the evidence substantially.

The baseline comparison does not establish the benefit of modeling token positions. The proposed predictor incorporates the known cosine schedule, whereas the baselines are simple power, reciprocal, and logarithmic functions. A direct aggregate-loss predictor using the same logarithmic–cosine construction is an essential ablation. The power-law baseline is also labeled 'Exponential' without a precise equation.

The conclusion that position weighting is unnecessary exceeds the evidence. Equation 16 follows from imposing constant positional parameters; equal absolute loss reductions do not establish optimal gradient weighting. The experiments test only three fixed suppression schemes introduced after 100B tokens, with small, mixed accuracy changes and no reported uncertainty. They support a narrower claim that these particular interventions show no consistent benefit.

Generality remains uncertain across training horizons, learning-rate schedules, and data mixtures because the experiments use one training recipe and two sizes of the same architecture family. Moreover, The Pile includes Gutenberg/PG-19 data, so the PG-19 evaluation does not establish transfer to an unseen domain; the OOD characterization needs qualification.

Reproducibility is insufficiently documented. The promised appendix containing fitted parameters is absent from the supplied PDF. Nonlinear fitting procedures, initialization and constraints, and batch size needed to translate warmup steps into tokens are not specified adequately. The transition point is also inconsistent: 40% of 400B tokens implies 160B, whereas Section 4.1 states 120B.

The novelty framing overstates the absence of prior temporal analysis: Kaplan et al. already study training-step learning curves. The contribution should be distinguished as a particular position-dependent, schedule-conditioned empirical model. Overall, the descriptive observations are promising, but forecasting validation and reproducibility require important revisions before a clear Findings recommendation.
